column1: # libbox gomobile ABI compatibility contract.
# # What this file is
# The machine-readable form of "these libbox methods return a bound *StringBox, and every
# client call site must read it through an accessor". scripts/ci/check-libbox-abi.sh reads
# it and fails when any of the layers disagrees with it.
# # Why it exists
# A bare `string` result puts a Go pointer into the `__attribute__((packed))` gomobile
# result frame and can throw `fatal error: bulkBarrierPreWrite: unaligned arguments`, which
# kills the process and cannot be recovered. Migrating the Go signature is therefore only one
# of three layers, and the easiest one: the generated binding and every Kotlin/Swift call site
# have to move with it. A build can regenerate libbox.aar successfully and still ship a client
# whose gitlink points at a revision calling the old ABI. Regenerating an AAR is a green light
# for the binding and says nothing whatsoever about the call sites. This contract is what
# makes that state a failure instead of a PASS.
# # Format
# One record per line, tab-separated. A line whose first non-blank character is '#' is a
# comment; blank lines are ignored.
#   col 1  go-owner     the bound type the declaration is attributed to by the surface
#                       scanner in experimental/libbox/gomobile_surface_test.go, i.e. the
#                       EXPORTED type name for an interface method, or "-" for a package-level
#                       function. This is the scanner's key, not the receiver's type name:
#                       BridgeSession.Name is implemented on the unexported
#                       *bridgeServiceSession, but a client reaches it through BridgeSession.
#   col 2  go-method    Go method / function name, exactly as declared.
#   col 3  javamethod   method name in the generated Java binding (lowerCamelCase).
#   col 4  kotlin-res   extended grep -E alternation matching the RECEIVER expression only,
#                       i.e. everything before `.<javamethod>(`. Used by the Kotlin scan.
#   col 5  swift-res    same, for the Swift/ObjC scan.
#   col 6  evidence     the call sites that were moved; for the reader, not parsed.
# A record asserts, and the gate enforces, all of:
#   1. the surface scanner still attributes a declaration to <go-owner>.<go-method> AND
#      classifies its result as a bound object rather than a pointer-bearing bare
#      string/[]byte. This is what catches a revert of the migration;
#   2. the Go declaration's result really is `*StringBox`;
#   3. the generated Java binding declares the method returning
#      `io.nekohasekai.libbox.StringBox` and does not declare a bare `java.lang.String`
#      result for it;
#   4. every call site in the pinned Android/Apple client source whose receiver matches
#      col 4 / col 5 reads the result through a migrated accessor - `.value`, or the Kotlin
#      `StringBox?.unwrap` extension. A call that reads it any other way is an old-ABI call
#      site and fails;
#   5. the client gitlinks are the revisions the contract was verified against.
# # Why the receiver is spelled out instead of matching the bare method name
# `name`, `address`, `mask` and `message` are extremely common identifiers and the clients'
# own types carry methods with those names too (RemoteControlManager.remoteServer.value,
# CardGroup.values(), CryptoSwift's `String.bytes`, ...). A scan keyed on the bare method name
# reports those as violations forever, which trains a reader to ignore the gate. The receiver
# patterns are anchored on how the bound object is actually reached in each client.
# # Adding a record
# When another method is migrated off a bare-string result, add it here AND move the client
# call sites, in the same change. Adding a record without moving the call sites makes this
# gate fail, which is the point.
# go-owner
